ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Mary Shelley

code.originalText: Primary care visit for headaches with episodes of numbness and weakness of the right hand and leg

text.paragraph: Primary care visit for headaches with episodes of numbness and weakness of the right hand and leg [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: Headaches for about two years, now most mornings, and frightening spells in which her right hand and leg go numb and weak for a few minutes. [S]
Afraid of being told it is "only nerves" again, and of losing the use of the hand she writes with. [S]
Has lived through many losses and does not want her son burdened; wants to understand everything and decide for herself. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Mary Wollstonecraft Godwin was born in London on August 30, 1797, the only child of the writer Mary Wollstonecraft and the philosopher William Godwin. [D]
Her mother died in London on September 10, 1797, eleven days after the birth, of puerperal fever; her father wrote that the placenta had been retained and had to be removed by hand. [D]
Her first child, a daughter born prematurely in February 1815, died after a few days. [D]
She began the tale that became Frankenstein in Switzerland in the summer of 1816, and Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus was published anonymously in January 1818, when she was 20. [D]
Her daughter Clara died in Italy in 1818, at about one year, and her son William died in Italy in June 1819, at three; she then had no living children. [D]
Her son Percy Florence, born in November 1819, was the only one of her four children to survive childhood. [D]
In June 1822 she nearly died of hemorrhage after a miscarriage about three months into a pregnancy; her husband stopped the bleeding by placing her in ice baths. [D]

In July 1822 her husband, the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, drowned while sailing in the Gulf of Spezia, leaving her a widow before she was 25, with a son of two; she decided to earn her living by her writing and by publishing his. [D]
She published the novels Valperga (1823) and The Last Man (1826), a revised Frankenstein (1831), and Rambles in Germany and Italy (1844). [D]

At about fourteen she had a very painful skin condition of one entire arm, treated with poultices; at times she could not move the arm and wore it in a sling. It has been interpreted as eczema, psoriasis, or chickenpox. [D]

In her journal in June 1840 she wrote that she had been long oppressed by care, disappointment, and ill health, and that lately ill health and extreme depression had marred what little she could do for others. [D]

From 1839 she had recurrent severe headaches of varying severity, site, and duration, with dizziness, pain in the legs, right hand, and right eye, brief episodes of partial paralysis of the right leg and hand, tremors, and convulsive seizures. Her physicians called the illness psychosomatic in 1842, a functional derangement of the nerves or brain in 1845, and neuralgia of the heart in 1846. [D]
From 1846 to 1851 she lived at 24 Chester Square, Belgravia, London, and spent time at Field Place in Sussex, the home of her son and his wife after their marriage in 1848. [D]

text.paragraph: 4 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: Painful skin disease of one whole arm at about fourteen, treated with poultices and a sling; diagnosis uncertain
Four pregnancies carried to birth, the first ending in a premature delivery
Miscarriage at about three months with near-fatal hemorrhage, treated with ice baths

Recurrent severe headaches with dizziness, pain in the right hand and eye, transient partial paralysis of the right leg and hand, tremors, and convulsive seizures; called psychosomatic, a derangement of the nerves, and neuralgia by her physicians
Ill health and extreme depression recorded in her journal

tr.td: Died of puerperal fever eleven days after giving birth to her, after a retained placenta

list.item: Occupation: novelist, travel writer, and editor of her late husband's poems; working on a new novel and a travel book; writes by hand each morning [S]
Bereavement history: her mother died days after her birth; widowed in her twenties; three of her four children died in infancy or early childhood; a near-fatal miscarriage; one adult son, married [S]
Lives alone in a London house; spends some weeks at her son's country home; drives occasionally [S]
Never smoker; a glass of wine with dinner a few times a week; walks most days; no other substance use [S]
Supports: a few close friends, her publisher, and her son and daughter-in-law; finds meaning in her work [S]
Reproductive history: four live births and one miscarriage; menopause at 50; no hormone therapy [S]

tr.td: Acetaminophen 500 mg oral tablet, two tablets (1000 mg) by mouth up to three times a day as needed for headache or wound pain, no more than 3000 mg a day
Two tablets up to every 8 hours as needed

S — Synthetic presenting concern at the index visit, superseded by the MRI and EEG diagnosis; her documented headaches with transient right-sided paralysis from 1839 are echoed.

value.displayName: Other symptoms and signs involving the nervous system

list.item: Headaches, worse in the morning, for about two years, with episodes over six months of tingling and weakness of the right hand and leg lasting a few minutes, one with twitching of the right fingers and one with difficulty finding words; mild right-hand weakness on examination; cause not yet established; urgent MRI and EEG booked: active, confirmed [S]

Urgent MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium, with diffusion imaging and MR angiography of the head and neck, within three days; EEG within a week; ECG, blood count, metabolic panel, calcium, and TSH today; headache and episode diary. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Central Nervous System Cancers, Version 2.2025 (2025); Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults. Krumholz A, et al. Neurology 2015;84(16):1705-1713 (2015) [S]

Safety now: no driving until the cause is known and her seizures are controlled for the period her state requires; showers rather than baths, no swimming alone, and no work at heights; seizure first aid explained; come at once for a longer episode, weakness that does not recover, or a severe sudden headache. Guideline: Evidence-based guideline: Management of an unprovoked first seizure in adults. Krumholz A, et al. Neurology 2015;84(16):1705-1713 (2015) [S]

Neurosurgery consultation if the MRI shows a structural lesion, to explain the options and their risks to her and plan treatment with her. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Central Nervous System Cancers, Version 2.2025 (2025) [S]

Grief and mood: a grief history, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at each visit, and the neuro-oncology counselor offered; no assumption that her symptoms are "nerves". Guideline: Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (depression screening and PHQ-9 follow-up) (2026) [S]

Protect her writing: occupational therapy assessment of hand function if weakness persists, and voice dictation as a backup. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Central Nervous System Cancers, Version 2.2025 (2025) [S]
Referral to neurosurgery, Cassius Ferreira-Lindgren, MD, ordered 2026-03-03 [S]
